insights:
The most glaring problem with this algorithm is its extreme passivity: 142 out of 170 trials (83.5%) produced NO trades, and of the last 10 trials, 8 were no-trade days. This is a day trading algorithm that refuses to trade. The scoring threshold is clearly too high or the scoring model is too conservative — the average composite score is 62.7 but the system is filtering out nearly everything. Meanwhile, the 28 trials that DID produce trades had a 28.6% win rate, which is poor but the profit factor of 20.16 suggests the winners are massive relative to losers. This means the algorithm CAN identify outsized winners but is either (a) not finding enough of them or (b) filtering them out with excessive conservatism.

Looking at the last 10 trials specifically: Trials 161 and 162 were the only ones that produced trades, and BOTH scored 50 with 0% win rates. Trial 161 went long LRCX and SMH in a 'rotation' regime with a bullish briefing — this is directionally coherent but the rotation classification (54% confidence) with high appetite (71) should have flagged this as a momentum-chasing setup rather than a high-conviction entry. Trial 162 went short AMAT and SMH in a rotation regime with a BEARISH briefing — here the briefing and recommendations were aligned (bearish → short semis) but the regime was classified as 'rotation' at only 35% confidence with moderate appetite (40). The system is making correlated bets (two semi plays in 161, two semi shorts in 162) which violates diversification principles and amplifies sector-specific risk. The remaining 8 trials all defaulted to 'No trades' despite several having clear directional setups — Trial 163 was risk-on at 58% confidence with 71 appetite and a bullish briefing, yet produced nothing. Trial 166 was risk-on at 61% confidence with a bullish briefing describing a 'powerful tech-led relief rally' and STILL produced no trades. These are precisely the environments where the algorithm should be generating high-conviction long entries.

The dimension predictive power data reveals a remarkably flat distribution: all seven dimensions cluster between 69.1 and 72.5 out of 100, with only 12 samples each. This is insufficient data to draw reliable conclusions, but the slight edge of timingUrgency (72.5) and catalystClarity (72.3) over volumeLiquidity (69.1) and marketAlignment (69.3) suggests the algorithm should lean more into catalyst-driven, time-sensitive setups rather than trying to perfectly align with broad market direction. The weight evolution shows persistent instability — weights oscillate trial to trial without converging, indicating the learning algorithm is overfitting to recent outcomes rather than building stable priors.

The best 5 trials share a critical pattern: ALL were single-trade days with 100% win rates. The algorithm performs best when it has ONE high-conviction idea, not two or three. The worst trials (138, 161, 162) all had 2+ trades, often correlated. This strongly suggests the system should be capped at 1 trade per day maximum, and that the second trade is typically a dilution of conviction rather than genuine diversification. The worst trial (75) had 3 trades in energy/materials — pure sector concentration masquerading as a portfolio.

The regime classifier is underconfident and potentially miscalibrated. In the last 10 trials, confidence ranged from 34-61%, with 6 of 10 below 45%. A classifier that is below 50% confident most of the time is providing almost no actionable signal. The 'range-bound' classification appeared 4 times and 'rotation' 3 times — these are essentially 'I don't know' labels that the algorithm correctly refuses to trade on, but the problem is these labels may be masking tradeable environments. Trial 166 (risk-on, 61%, powerful rally) and Trial 163 (risk-on, 58%, pressing higher) were clearly actionable days that the system left on the table.
strategyChanges: Cap maximum trades per day at 1. The best trials were all single-trade days; multi-trade days (138, 161, 162, 75) are the worst performers. If two candidates score above threshold, take ONLY the highest-scoring one.

Prohibit correlated sector bets: never recommend two tickers from the same sector or ETF family (e.g., LRCX+SMH, AMAT+SMH, MSFT+AMD). Implement a sector-deduplication filter that forces the second pick to be in a different GICS sector.

Lower the composite score threshold from ~65-70 to 58. The algorithm is passing on 83.5% of trading days, which means it's missing high-quality setups. The risk-on days with 58-61% regime confidence and bullish briefings (Trials 163, 166) should absolutely generate trades.

When regime is classified as 'risk-on' with confidence >55% AND briefing is 'bullish', force the system to generate at least one long candidate. The current pipeline allows risk-on+bullish to produce zero trades, which is a logic failure.

Add a regime confidence floor: if regime confidence is below 40%, override to 'uncertain' and only allow mean-reversion or volatility plays, not directional bets. The 34-35% confidence 'rotation' and 'range-bound' labels are noise.

Stabilize weight evolution by using exponential moving average of weights across trials with decay factor 0.95, preventing wild oscillations between trials. Current weights are effectively random-walking.
blindSpots: Relief rally / mean-reversion setups after multi-day selloffs: Trial 167 had 4 consecutive down days with stress=20 and appetite=30, a textbook oversold bounce setup, but produced no trades. The algorithm has no mean-reversion signal.

Holiday/half-session dynamics: Trial 168 (July 3rd half-session) was classified as rotation with no trades. Low-volume half-sessions have unique dynamics (drift higher, low volatility) that the regime classifier doesn't account for.

Post-earnings momentum: Several trials overlap with earnings season but the algorithm doesn't appear to weight fresh earnings catalysts differently from other catalysts. The best trial (PLTR short, Trial 8) likely capitalized on post-earnings overextension.

The algorithm never seems to trade volatility products or use VIX-related signals despite having stress indicators. When stress is elevated (Trial 167, stress=20), vol products offer asymmetric setups the system completely ignores.
Sector rotation identification is poor: the system correctly identifies 'rotation' but doesn't specify WHICH sectors are rotating INTO vs OUT OF, making the label useless for trade generation.
pipelineIssues: SIGNAL → REGIME disconnect: The regime classifier outputs low-confidence labels (34-41%) that are effectively noise, but the trade recommendation engine treats them as hard constraints. A 34% confidence 'range-bound' should not suppress all trading — it should widen the opportunity set to include both long and short candidates.

REGIME → BRIEFING inconsistency: Trial 161 had regime='rotation' but briefing='bullish'; Trial 162 had regime='rotation' but briefing='bearish'. The briefing is contradicting the regime, and the trade recs follow the briefing not the regime. The pipeline needs a reconciliation step: if regime and briefing disagree, flag the conflict and reduce position size rather than proceeding with full conviction.

BRIEFING → RECOMMENDATIONS gap: Trials 163 and 166 had bullish briefings with risk-on regimes and generated ZERO trade recommendations. This is the most critical pipeline failure — the upstream signals are correct but the downstream trade generation engine is too restrictive. The recommendation engine needs to be re-parameterized to be responsive to strong regime+briefing alignment.

OUTCOMES scoring is broken: All last 10 trials show outcomes=[N/A], meaning the feedback loop from trade outcomes back to the scoring model is not functioning. Without outcome data, the weight evolution is adjusting blind. This must be fixed immediately — the algorithm cannot learn without outcome feedback.

WEIGHT EVOLUTION is unstable: Weights have not converged after 170 trials. The learning rate is too high, causing weights to oscillate. Additionally, with only 12 samples per dimension, the predictive power estimates have wide confidence intervals (~±10 points), meaning the current weight adjustments are based on statistically insignificant differences.

161.reasoning: The bullish briefing and high appetite (71) support a long semi play, but ONLY one position — drop SMH to avoid correlated sector doubling. LRCX as a single name has more alpha potential than the ETF. Tighter stop (-2%) given rotation regime uncertainty.

162.reasoning: The briefing explicitly noted defensive rotation into Healthcare and Real Estate. Instead of shorting semis (fighting a sector that could bounce), go LONG the sector rotating INTO favor. XLV long captures the defensive rotation theme directly with lower risk than a short position in a volatile sector.

163.reasoning: Risk-on at 58% confidence, 71 appetite, bullish briefing noting semis and cyclicals leading. This was a clear trade day the algorithm inexplicably passed on. NVDA as the semi bellwether with highest liquidity is the clean single-name expression of the risk-on theme.

164.reasoning: Range-bound with elevated stress (16) and third consecutive S&P down day. In a volatile, range-bound environment, GLD offers a defensive hedge with trend support. Low-correlation trade when directional equity conviction is low.

165.reasoning: Briefing noted mega-cap tech and semis surging post-election. Despite range-bound regime label (41% confidence — essentially noise), the sector signal was clear: tech leadership. QQQ long captures the bifurcated market's strong side. The regime classifier's low confidence should not have blocked this trade.

166.reasoning: Risk-on at 61% confidence, bullish briefing describing 'powerful tech-led relief rally' with S&P up 1.68%. This is the clearest long setup in the entire last-10 batch. META as a mega-cap tech leader with high beta to relief rallies was the obvious play. The algorithm's failure to trade here represents its single biggest missed opportunity.

167.reasoning: Four consecutive down days, stress=20 (highest in the last 10), appetite=30. This is a textbook mean-reversion setup. SPY long with a tight stop (-1.5%) captures the oversold bounce. The bearish briefing was backward-looking; the forward-looking signal was the extreme oversold condition.

168.reasoning: July 3rd half-session with constructive surface, S&P up 0.51%. Half-sessions before holidays have a well-documented upward drift bias with compressed volatility. SPY long with a modest target (+0.3-0.5%) and tight stop is a high-probability low-risk setup the system should exploit.

169.reasoning: Range-bound, neutral-to-contradictory signals. When equity signals are mixed, look for cross-asset opportunities. The 'deeply contradictory posture' in equities often resolves via a flight to quality. TLT long is the non-correlated play when the equity signal is genuinely unclear.

170.reasoning: Bearish briefing with second consecutive S&P down day and defensive posture. Rather than going short (which the system correctly avoided), go long the defensive sector benefiting from the rotation. XLU captures the flight-to-safety flow with lower risk than a directional equity short.
